_meta.title: What Phase 0 could not retrieve, and exactly what closes each item
_meta.note: Two categories. BLOCKING items stop a specific Phase 1-3 deliverable and need a human action. NON-BLOCKING items are claims that must simply not ship until sourced — the tool works without them.
_meta.common_cause: The dominant blocker is binary spreadsheets. Federal agencies increasingly publish distributional data ONLY as .xlsx/.xls, and this session's tooling reads text and HTML but returns unparseable binary for those. Every such item closes with a manual download.
_meta.revised: 2026-08-17 (third revision). Daniel downloaded the source spreadsheets; B1, B2, B3, B4, B7 and B9 are all CLOSED. B5 (PolicyEngine) and B6/B8 (minor) remain.
_meta.remaining: B5 PolicyEngine validation (substitute benchmarks in place). B6 withdrawn as unnecessary. B8 absolute-mobility cohort array (both endpoints already sourced). NOTHING now blocks Phase 1 or Phase 2.

blocking.what: CBO 2022 average household income by quintile (before and after transfers and taxes), the top-1% dollar values, and the average federal tax rate for the SECOND, MIDDLE, and FOURTH quintiles.
blocking.why_it_matters: Gameplan §4 Act 2 output 2: the by-class chart is ALWAYS VISIBLE and is Daniel's stated core requirement. Three of its five quintile bars cannot be drawn without this file. The lowest quintile (1.4%), highest quintile (23.2%), and top 1% (31.5%) ARE available from published prose; the middle three are not.
blocking.why_blocked: CBO publication 61911 contains NO numbered data tables — every income-by-quintile value exists only as a chart in the PDF and as numbers in the supplemental Excel. Both .xlsx files return unparseable binary.
blocking.human_action: Download 61911-supplemental-data.xlsx, open it, and read the 2022 rows. Needed: average income before transfers and taxes by quintile + top 1%; average income after transfers and taxes by the same groups; average federal tax rate for all five quintiles and the top 1%; and the full 1979-2022 historical series by quintile (which also closes B4). Drop the values into a CSV or paste them into a session. Estimated effort: 5-10 minutes.
blocking.do_not_do: Do NOT chart-read the PDF. An automated read of Figure 1 suggested roughly $20k/$60k/$110k/$180k/$450k by quintile, at best plus or minus $10,000. Those are NOT data and must never be published as CBO figures. Do not interpolate the three missing tax rates either.
blocking.note: CBO quintiles contain equal numbers of PEOPLE, not equal numbers of households, so household counts cannot be derived by dividing.
blocking.second_pass_note: A dedicated pass tried six routes and failed on the 2022 values: CBO has no interactive/JSON endpoint for this series; the 2022 report contains no tables and no appendix (it outsources definitions to the 2021 edition); no secondary source republishes the quintile dollar table; CBO offers no CSV alternative. What the pass DID recover, from prose in earlier editions: 2021 lowest quintile $22,500 before / $48,700 after and highest $418,100 before / $316,800 after; 2020 lowest $21,900/$45,800 and highest $357,800/$275,700; 2019 lowest $23,800, middle $81,800, highest $332,100, top 1% ~$2.0M, top 0.01% ~$43.0M; 2018 lowest $22,500/$37,700, middle $77,500, highest $321,700. CRITICAL: two independent fetches of the 2021 edition's Appendix C TABLES returned mutually contradictory numbers for the second/middle/fourth quintiles, so only prose-stated values are trusted. The second and fourth quintiles are unrecovered for EVERY year.
blocking.phase1_workaround: Phase 1 CAN build a credible class chart today using CBO's 1979-2005 series (all five quintiles, from series-arrays.json) for the historical panel, and the 2019 prose values for a recent snapshot. What it cannot do is render 2022 quintile dollar values or the 2022 second/middle/fourth quintile tax rates.
blocking.resolution: CLOSED 2026-08-17. 61911-supplemental-data.xlsx parsed. Recovered FAR more than the 2022 values: all 12 CBO tables run 1979-2022, including average household income by source, average federal tax rates BY TAX COMPONENT, income shares and tax shares, for all five quintiles plus 81-90th, 91-95th, 96-99th and top 1 percent. Extracted to data/cbo-distribution.json. THIS ALSO CLOSES B4.

blocking.what: IRS SOI Table 3.5 (TY2023), 'All Returns: Tax Generated, by Rate and by Size of Adjusted Gross Income' — the distribution of income taxed at each marginal rate bracket.
blocking.why_it_matters: Layer 1 applies rate and base changes across the income distribution. Without bracket-level detail the top-rate slider with an adjustable threshold — Act 2's headline lever — cannot be computed. The available fallback (SOI TY2022 preliminary, in history-series.json) tops out at a single '$250,000 or more' bucket, which is far too coarse.
blocking.why_blocked: IRS publishes these only as .xls. No HTML or PDF equivalent exists for TY2023; the Pub 1304 full PDF is available only through TY2022.
blocking.human_action: Download 23in35tr.xls at minimum. If the engine also wants AGI-class aggregates, add 23in11si.xls. Export each to CSV.
blocking.correction: THE GAMEPLAN AND DOSSIER NAME THE WRONG TABLE. Table 3.4 is 'Tax Classified by Both the Marginal Rate and Each Rate at Which Tax Was Computed, BY FILING STATUS.' The by-AGI-size table the engine needs is TABLE 3.5. Fix this in the gameplan.
blocking.context: TY2023 is the latest complete published SOI year (Pub 1304 tables released March 2026). High-income tables lag further — TY2022 is the latest for those.
blocking.resolution: CLOSED 2026-08-17. 23in35tr.xls parsed (needed xlrd 1.2.0 in the container; the device lacks xlrd). 25 AGI classes to $10M+, with number of returns, income taxed and tax generated at every ordinary rate (10/12/22/24/32/35/37) and every capital-gains rate (0/15/20/25/28). Extracted to data/soi-table-3-5.json.

blocking.what: IRS SOI Table 4.1 (TY2023) — top 0.1% and top 0.01% AGI thresholds and average tax rates.
blocking.why_it_matters: Gameplan §2 scope: 'Quintiles + top 1%/0.1% everywhere.' The top 0.1% bar cannot be drawn from published secondary sources — neither Tax Foundation nor NTU breaks out below the top 1%.
blocking.human_action: Download and read the top 0.1% / 0.01% rows.
blocking.workaround_available: The top-1% row IS available second-hand and is loaded in history-series.json > soi_percentiles. Phase 1 can proceed with quintiles + top 1%, deferring the 0.1% bar. Note also that CBO publishes total-federal-rate detail for the 99th-99.9th (31.0%), 99.9th-99.99th (32.6%), and top 0.01% (31.2%) via Tax Foundation's reading — so a partial sub-1% story is tellable today.
blocking.scope_decision_needed: If B3 stays blocked, either ship v1 with quintiles + top 1% only and say so, or defer. Do not fabricate the 0.1% bar.
blocking.resolution: CLOSED 2026-08-17. 23in41ts.xlsx parsed. Recovered TY2001-2023 (not just 2023) across eight measures, down to the TOP 0.001 PERCENT. Extracted to data/soi-percentiles.json.

blocking.what: CBO effective federal tax rate by quintile, full series 1979-2022.
blocking.why_blocked: Same Excel as B1. Additionally, THE DOSSIER'S CITATION IS WRONG: cbo.gov/publication/61259 is 'H.R. 1491, Disaster Related Extension of Deadlines Act' (2025-03-24), a bill cost estimate with no distributional data. That citation must be removed from the dossier and the gameplan.
blocking.human_action: Same download as B1 — the historical tab of 61911-supplemental-data.xlsx carries the full 1979-2022 series.
blocking.what_is_available_today: Only fragments, all secondary: top 1% 'ranging between 25 and 35 percent since 1979'; bottom quintile 'averaged about 10.6 percent in the 1980s but has remained below 3 percent since 2007'; and the verified 2022 endpoints. The dossier's stated endpoints (top 1% ~33% in 1979 to ~30% in 2021; middle ~19% to ~13%) are UNVERIFIED and must not ship.
blocking.extra_warning: 2021 is a distorted pandemic year (the bottom 60% paid just 1.3% of federal taxes that year because of recovery rebate credits). 2022 is the correct endpoint, and its verified top-1% rate of 31.5% makes the dossier's 'declining to ~30%' narrative misleading.
blocking.resolution: CLOSED 2026-08-17 by the same file as B1 — cbo-distribution.json carries the full 1979-2022 series by group and by tax component.

blocking.severity: BLOCKS THE POLICYENGINE VALIDATION REQUIRED BY PHASE 0
blocking.what: Three static calculations validated against PolicyEngine: top rate +2pp, capital gains +5pp, 199A repeal.
blocking.why_blocked: PolicyEngine's REST API requires an HTTP POST to create a parameterized reform, which this build environment could not issue. The one stored policy matching a target reform (id 32979, capital gains 23.8%→28.8%) returned status 'computing' on every poll and never resolved. GET /us/metadata exceeds 48MB and cannot be retrieved, so parameter paths could not be confirmed either.
blocking.parameter_paths_unverified: gov.irs.income.bracket.rates.7 (top rate) and gov.irs.deductions.qbi.* (199A) are INFERRED, not confirmed. Check them against /us/metadata before scripting.
blocking.important_caveat: PolicyEngine does NOT model capital gains realization responses ('we are now working on adding capital gains responses'). It would substantially overstate revenue from the capital gains reform. Use it to validate the top-rate and 199A levers; use the elasticity literature for capital gains.
blocking.substitute_in_place: External benchmarks from other shops are loaded in scenarios.json > validation_benchmarks, including three POST-OBBBA figures from the Tax Foundation 2026 Options Guide. Phase 2 can test against those. This does not fully discharge the gameplan requirement — see the build report.
blocking.second_pass_note: Substitute post-OBBBA benchmarks are loaded in scenarios.json > validation_benchmarks. Still worth running locally.

blocking.severity: CLOSED AS UNNECESSARY — do not chase
blocking.why_blocked: The two Census reports containing them (P60-241, P60-244) live only on www2.census.gov, which is robots-disallowed. The www.census.gov content/dam mirrors 404.
blocking.note: 2011-2024 is fully sourced (14 points). The SPM story — record low in 2021, snap-back in 2022 — is entirely tellable without 2009-2010.
blocking.why_withdrawn: The Census page hosting tableB-2.xlsx returns 404, and the two years it would buy (2009, 2010) are not needed. The SPM argument — record low 7.8% in 2021 during a recession because of transfers, snapping back to 12.4% in 2022 when they lapsed — lives entirely inside the sourced 2011-2024 range. The tool should simply state that its SPM series begins in 2011.

blocking.why_blocked: Saez's update lives only in TabFig2024.xlsx. wid.world/bulk_download returns 404 and api.wid.world returns 403.
blocking.note: 1913-1998 IS sourced from the original QJE Table II. And the WID/DINA variant is complete 1913-2024. So the tool can still show two of three series in full and the third through 1998.
blocking.resolution: CLOSED 2026-08-17. TabFig2024.xlsx parsed. Piketty-Saez fiscal-income top shares now run 1913-2024 in BOTH capital-gains variants (Tables A1 and A3), replacing the 1913-1998 QJE extract.

blocking.what: IRS SOI estate tax filing-year Table 1, FILING YEARS 2023 and 2024 only: total returns filed, and number or share taxable.
blocking.why_it_matters: series-arrays.json > estate_returns currently runs 2001-2022 (108,071 filed / 51,766 taxable in 2001 down to 8,130 / 3,171 in 2022). Two more years makes it current. The collapse is already legible without them.
blocking.why_blocked: IRS publishes the filing-year tables only as .xlsx.
blocking.optional_extra: Filing years 1995-2000 would add a pre-EGTRRA baseline. Low value; skip unless free.
blocking.basis_warning: This series is FILING YEAR, not year of death. Most returns filed in year T are for deaths in T-1. TPC's year-of-death projections (~7,100 filed / ~4,000 taxable for 2023 deaths) are on a DIFFERENT basis and must not be plotted on the same line.
blocking.resolution: CLOSED 2026-08-17. IRS SOI estate Table 1 for filing years 2023 and 2024 parsed: FY2023 9,024 filed / 3,690 taxable; FY2024 7,195 filed / 2,663 taxable. Those two years use IRS's own taxable count, not the derived one.
